subject: Feedback on paper about rstanarm's informative prior on R2

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Feedback on paper about rstanarm's informative prior on R2
parts:
The stan_lm function in rstanarm implements a linear model with regularizing priors driven by prior beliefs about the R^2. This has been confusing to many users and pretty much everyone except for Ben (who had the idea for this cool prior). In light of the confusion, I've written a rough draft of a paper about the prior and I would very much appreciate some feedback. The latest version is attached as a pdf. You can also find the pdf as well as the raw .tex file and R code for the graphics on GitHub in my R2prior repository. 

The paper is pretty short (9 pages or so) so it should be a quick read.

Thanks, 

Jonah

- Also for good practice on that page please use display() to summarize the fitted model.
A

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: Feedback on paper about rstanarm's informative prior on R2
parts:
The draft made R^2 prior more clear for me. Here are few quick comments

- I just remembered that one of our papers http://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0029115
has a discussion on prior beliefs about the R^2 using similar (but different) approach as the approach by Guan and Stephens (2011). The real data experiment had n=3 895, p=1 051 811.

- Could you describe more about the properties of the implied marginal prior? Now you write that it gets more concentrated, but I'm interested how the tail shape behaves or how would the implied marginal prior on the amount of shrinkage look like (cf. horseshoe prior paper)

- In the prior for R^2, the first parameter is K/2 and the second is eta. Information about the location of R^2 is used to choose eta. How is the amount of prior information controlled (weakly informative vs strong information)? If you think it is not needed, it would helpfull to comment anyway, why there is no another parameter for controlling how strong the prior information is about specific location of R^2.

- In the experiment you write "R^2 should be fairly small". How did you decide 0.2 is good value for fairly small? Why not 0.1 or 0.3? Is the result sensitive to this?

Aki

On Monday, March 28, 2016 at 3:27:02 PM UTC-4, Aki Vehtari wrote:
- Could you describe more about the properties of the implied marginal prior? Now you write that it gets more concentrated, but I'm interested how the tail shape behaves or how would the implied marginal prior on the amount of shrinkage look like (cf. horseshoe prior paper)

For an unknown correlation matrix among the K -1 predictors (the paper / vignette redefines this as K predictors), the 1-dimensional PDF of any standardized coefficient is "known" to be


which is not very intuitive. The characteristic function is also known and real (so the odd moments are zero if they exist) so


We also know the characteristic function (but not the density) of the full-conditional distribution, which may provide some intuition

- In the prior for R^2, the first parameter is K/2 and the second is eta. Information about the location of R^2 is used to choose eta. How is the amount of prior information controlled (weakly informative vs strong information)? If you think it is not needed, it would helpfull to comment anyway, why there is no another parameter for controlling how strong the prior information is about specific location of R^2.

Yeah, I started out thinking about the traditional case where the number of observations was large relative to a fixed number of predictors, and you get this Beta(K/2, eta) prior on the R^2. But more generally K could be the rank of the design matrix in the case where there are more predictors than observations or K could even be the expected number of non-zero coefficients. We haven't worked out the case yet where there are more predictors than observations.
- In the experiment you write "R^2 should be fairly small". How did you decide 0.2 is good value for fairly small? Why not 0.1 or 0.3? Is the result sensitive to this?

The coefficients are a bit sensitive but mostly because there are something like 25 observations and 12 parameters. I don't think the estimate of the average treatment effect is very sensitive to this. In general, the data are informative about the R^2.

Thanks,
Ben
